Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Similar cars' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger unless there is a very specific undisclosed trauma context; it reads as a transport/accident-associated cue rather than illness-related.

'Related people/known people' can occur around illness trauma, but paired with other selected triggers and threat items it suggests an interpersonal or assault-like threat context more than a medical illness context.

Scanning for exits is much more characteristic of fear of external attack or entrapment than of trauma centered on life-threatening illness, and is difficult to connect coherently to the rest of an illness-based profile.
Reacting to unexpected nearby movement as if in danger is also more typical of assault/combat-type threat expectations than illness trauma, creating a mismatch with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Being Praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless paired with illness-specific meanings elsewhere (e.g., praise for surviving, coping, or returning to function). No corresponding appraisal or memory content makes this trigger clinically coherent here.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Scanning Exits' and 'Startle to Movement' imply a danger formulation centered on assault/attack or external interpersonal threat, which is difficult to reconcile with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you' similarly reflects fear of intentional human harm rather than recurrence of illness, bodily catastrophe, medical procedures, or death from disease. This is poorly aligned with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Going Out' would be coherent if linked to infection fears, collapse in public, or medical reminders, but those meanings are not represented in the trigger, threat, or appraisal items selected. As written, it appears to address a different threat context than the rest of the profile.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'related people' as a trigger is plausible, but the profile otherwise anchors triggers strongly in medical reminders and bodily danger rather than interpersonal threat. This item becomes hard to reconcile because the accompanying appraisal and threat items do not explain why known people specifically function as a major trigger.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' implies an interpersonal perpetrator-based worldview. That is difficult to align with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness, especially when the rest of the profile centers medical cues, sleep disturbance, startle, and physical reactivity rather than harm from other people. A more illness- or vulnerability-focused appraisal would fit better.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, medical triggers like needles, drips, and procedures are coherent, but alcohol smell is not plausibly linked to the trauma context unless there is additional undisclosed treatment context; it stands out as a hard-to-explain trigger relative to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a 19-year-old male with life-threatening illness trauma. The other appraisals center on bodily vulnerability and loss of meaning, whereas a failed core-role appraisal implies a specific disrupted identity or responsibility that is otherwise absent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out
issues.explanation: Avoiding going out is weakly connected to the rest of the selected items. The profile is dominated by medical reminders and internal threat/bodily vulnerability, so broad avoidance of leaving home lacks a clear clinical target here and is not well explained by the trigger-threat-appraisal pattern shown.

vignette:
Evan had been nineteen for only a few months when a routine medical crisis turned into the kind of experience that still organized his days long after the immediate danger had passed. He was a European American young man in a relationship, and before the illness he had been building a life that felt ordinary and forward-moving: he worked as a counselor, spent much of his day sitting with other people's problems, and imagined that his own future would continue to open up in a similar way. Then he became seriously ill, and the hospital became the center of his world. He remembered the cold shine of the treatment room, the smell of antiseptic that seemed to cling to his clothes and throat, and the sight of needles, drips, and other equipment arranged around him with a clinical efficiency that made him feel less like a person than a body being managed. During examinations and procedures, he was aware of himself as frightened, alert, and waiting for something to go wrong. The memory of those moments did not stay in the past for him; it returned in fragments when he encountered even a small reminder of that time.

Now, months later, Evan described being thrown off balance by the most ordinary medical cues. If he passed a hospital entrance on the way to work, caught the sharp smell of antiseptic, or saw a drip stand in a waiting room, he felt his chest tighten and his attention lock onto the possibility that he might be taken back into that same helpless state. Needles were especially potent for him, not only when he saw them up close but even in images or in the sight of tubing and equipment that looked similar enough to draw his mind back. A physical examination could also bring the whole experience rushing into the present; he would become tense and watchful, as if his body already knew that something dangerous was about to happen before he had time to think it through. He had come to notice that the reaction was not limited to his thoughts. When something reminded him of the illness, he sometimes had strong physical responses that startled him with their force, leaving him shaky, keyed up, and certain that his body was reliving something it should have left behind.

Evan's sleep had gradually become one of the places where this played out most clearly. He would stay up very late, telling himself that there was always one more message to answer, one more thing to do, one more reason not to go to bed yet. In practice, the late nights gave him a temporary sense of control, and they also meant he did not have to lie still in the dark where his mind could wander back to the hospital. When he did try to sleep, he often had trouble falling asleep or would wake and find himself unable to settle again. The quiet of the night made him more aware of his own body, and that awareness was uncomfortable. He would lie there thinking that his body could not be trusted, because it had once failed him so completely and now seemed to react on its own, as if it were still in danger even when he was safely at home. That thought had become increasingly hard for him to shake. He spoke about his body as something unreliable, almost foreign, and he seemed distressed by the sense that it could still send him into panic before he had a chance to reassure himself.

As time went on, Evan began avoiding anything that might lead him back toward those reminders. He kept away from hospitals and ambulances whenever he could, and he also tried to avoid physical examinations, even when he knew they were routine. In his work, this meant taking routes that would not bring him near the local hospital and feeling a jolt of unease whenever a client or colleague mentioned medical issues. The avoidance extended into therapy as well. When sessions touched on the illness, he would try not to think about what had been discussed afterward, pushing the material away as soon as he left. Yet the effort to keep it at a distance left him feeling cut off from things that once mattered to him. He said that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, a statement he made quietly but with clear conviction, as though his illness had taken the future he had expected and left him unsure what was supposed to matter now.

His girlfriend noticed that he seemed more withdrawn and less able to relax, and Evan himself recognized that he was not simply "getting over it" the way he had hoped. Even at work, where he spent his days helping others, he found himself startled by sudden movement nearby, reacting as if he were in danger when a coworker came up behind him or a chair scraped too abruptly across the floor. Those moments embarrassed him because they felt so disproportionate, but they also reinforced his sense that his body was still on guard. He finally sought help because the pattern was spreading through too many parts of his life: sleep, work, relationships, and his own sense of purpose. What brought him in now was not only the persistence of the reminders but the fear that he would continue living as if the illness were still happening. More than anything, Evan hoped to feel at home in his own body again and to believe that his life could mean something, even after what it had been through.
